Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, Justice & Belonging
Wellbeing@VIS · Where this work began

Historical Context

The Wellbeing@VIS framework grew out of Dream 3 of our Road Map to our Destiny, fostering the wellbeing of our learners, and took shape during the COVID years of 2020 to 2021. It was formally launched alongside our CIS reaccreditation, which gave us the opportunity to take a deep dive into wellbeing and focus our resources on five Dream Projects.

At that time, wellbeing and DEIJB were pursued as two separate projects. Since then, our understanding has evolved. Today, wellbeing is the overarching commitment that shapes our whole community's culture, and DEIJB is understood as an essential component within it. Diversity, equity, inclusion, justice and belonging are part of what it means for every person at VIS to feel valued, safe and supported.

Wellbeing@VIS · 2025–2026

The Wellbeing Team

At VIS, wellbeing is the overarching umbrella for our whole community, and diversity, equity, inclusion, justice, and belonging (DEIJB) are how we build it. People are well when they feel safe, valued, and that they truly belong, so advancing our DEIJB goals is how we strengthen wellbeing for everyone. The Wellbeing Team carried this work forward, meeting weekly and guided by the DEIJB commitments.

DEIJB Commitments 2025–2026

In 2025–2026 our VIS staff community worked through four commitment areas, building shared language and practice around diversity, equity, inclusion, justice, and belonging.

1

Developing shared language & understanding

  • 1.1Clarity of what DEIJB is in our VIS local and global context.
  • 1.2Clarity of purpose and commitment to DEIJB.
  • 1.3Understanding that all humans hold bias that shapes how we think and interact.
  • 1.4Awareness of power and privilege.
  • 1.5Awareness of systems of oppression.
2

Identifying inequities, exclusion & injustice

  • 2.1Reviewing our CIS and Quaglia survey data.
  • 2.2Creating an internal survey to gather data from all community members.
  • 2.3Establishing the VIS Staff Advisory Council (VISSAC).
3

Reviewing systems, policies & documents

  • 3.1Reviewing the Board Policy Manual through an equity and inclusion lens.
  • 3.2Creating the Wellbeing Playbook to support our DEIJB principles and practices.
4

Using restorative approaches to harm

  • 4.1Understanding accountability, harm, intention, and impact.
  • 4.2Developing and understanding our restorative principles.
  • 4.3Noticing and naming mindsets and defensive behaviors.
  • 4.4Adopting the Warm Demander framework and restorative circles for accountable conversations.
Notes on commitment revisions 2022–2026

The DEIJB commitments have been reviewed and updated for 2025–2026 to reflect the school's current priorities, community feedback, and progress made since the original commitments were established in 2022. The notes below outline what was added, removed, or revised, and the reasoning behind each change.

Removed
DEIJB team commitment. Removed until a team is reassembled. The 2022–2023 DEIJ project team ended in June 2023 and was not continued after CIS/WASC accreditation.
3.2 Reviewing the recruiting process. Removed because the recruitment process has been reviewed and is now in the implementation phase.
2.3 Listening circles with staff. Removed to focus on collecting data via surveys for 2025–2026.
4.4 Normalizing challenging harmful words, actions, and views. Removed as specific restorative practices have now been adopted: the Warm Demander framework and restorative circles.
Added
1.1 Contextualizing DEIJB for our VIS local and global context.
2.2 Creating an internal survey to gather data from all community members. Added because current surveys are not accessible to all.
2.3 VISSAC, the VIS Staff Advisory Council. Added in response to community feedback to the Head of School regarding inclusivity and the need for voice and input in decision making.
4.2 Developing understanding of restorative principles.
Revised
Commitment 4. Framing shifted from “challenging” to using restorative approaches, reflecting the adoption of the Warm Demander framework and restorative circles.
DEIJB · Community Learning · September 2025

Community Learning Launch

Our whole staff community launched the year's wellbeing work with a session anchored in belonging, asking Who belongs here? and Whose wellbeing matters? The answer set the tone: all of us, all of ours.

What
  • Our whole staff community launched the year's wellbeing work with a session anchored in belonging.
  • Two questions framed the day: Who belongs here? and Whose wellbeing matters?
  • Staff revisited our existing Wellbeing@VIS statement, then chose one of three groups: belonging, wellbeing, or restorative principles.
Why
  • Our Wellbeing@VIS statement was first written in 2020 and had not been revisited in five years.
  • We wanted to know whether the words still describe the community we are becoming.
  • We wanted every voice, in Lao and in English, to help shape what comes next.
How
  • Staff read the existing Wellbeing statement together and responded to three prompts: what do you agree with, what is unclear, and what are we missing.
  • Choice groups then explored our definitions of belonging, wellbeing, and restorative principles in greater depth.
Outcomes
  • Our wellbeing statement was revised based on community feedback.
  • A new statement of belonging was drafted.
  • Restorative principles received feedback, and staff agreed on the need for a dedicated committee to carry the work forward.
  • A desire for one place to document these beliefs and definitions emerged, decision to create a Wellbeing Playbook.
DEIJB · Community Learning · September 2025

How Our Definitions Shifted

Following the launch, community feedback reshaped two foundational statements. Here is how our shared language for wellbeing and belonging grew.

Wellbeing
Before (2020)

At VIS we recognize that healthy social, emotional and physical wellbeing is essential for all learners to reach their full potential. We therefore aim to embed a culture within our community in which every person feels valued and emotionally supported in a healthy, safe and secure environment; has or can access tools to support their personal wellbeing; and is able and willing to support and respect the needs of others. This is a diverse culture that is equitable and inclusive, with justice at its core.

›
Now (2025)

At VIS, we define wellbeing as a state of holistic health characterized by balance and fulfillment across social, emotional, physical, mental, spiritual, occupational, financial, and environmental dimensions. It reflects an individual's experience of feeling seen, valued, and empowered within a supportive community. We believe wellbeing thrives in environments that promote equity, inclusivity, and a strong sense of belonging, enabling individuals to access resources that nurture their overall health and wellbeing.

What shifted
  • Broadened from three dimensions of wellbeing to eight, adding mental, spiritual, occupational, financial, and environmental.
  • Moved from learners reaching their potential toward a holistic picture of balance and fulfillment for everyone.
  • Added the language of feeling seen and empowered, not only valued and supported.
  • Named belonging explicitly as part of what allows wellbeing to thrive.
Belonging
Before

VIS had no statement of its own. Belonging was explored through the words of outside thinkers, who described it as the extent to which people feel appreciated, accepted, and treated fairly, and as a felt sense of safety, welcome, and wholeness.

›
Now (2025)

At VIS belonging means feeling seen, valued, and connected as a full member of our diverse learning community. It is the sense that each individual — student, staff member, and family — has an authentic place here, where their identity, culture, and perspectives are respected and contribute to our shared purpose. Belonging grows when we build trust across differences, honor our Lao host culture, and live our shared values of empathy, inclusion, and mutual respect.

What shifted
  • Moved from borrowed language to a definition written in our own community's words.
  • Centers each person as a full member whose identity, culture, and perspectives are respected.
  • Honors our Lao host culture and our multilingualism as part of how belonging is lived.
  • Connects belonging to relationships, learning, and collective care for one another.

Restorative Principles Committee

Staff volunteered to join a committee to develop VIS Restorative Principles that would give the whole community a shared language and a common set of guiding beliefs. The committee spent a semester drafting, listening, and revising principles based on restorative justice and community feedback.

Committee process
Aug 2025

A first draft existed by August 2025, and a school-wide PD session on September 3 generated the first round of community feedback.

Sept

Reviewed the school-wide feedback, agreed on recommended revisions, and planned how to gather wider input.

Oct

Finalized feedback tools and planned parent engagement, including a parent Community Inquiry Circle (CIC).

Nov

Held the parent CIC (Nov 20) and gathered feedback from all community members, collected on the committee's feedback Padlet.

Dec

A four-hour synthesis retreat where all the collected feedback was processed into decisions.

How feedback became decisions
A four-hour synthesis retreat, guided by one focus question: What changes will make these beliefs more clear and inclusive for our VIS community?
1

Context & framing

The committee reviewed the focus question and posted the four shared criteria used to judge every piece of feedback:

ClarityInclusivityRestorative alignmentActionability
2

Silent brainstorm

Each member individually read through the written feedback and captured one idea per sticky note.

3

Cluster

The sticky notes were posted and grouped into clusters of related ideas.

4

Name each cluster

Every cluster was given a short, clear title capturing the heart of the theme.

5

Reflect & decide

For each cluster, the team made a decision, documented the rationale against the four criteria, and noted how many sticky notes it represented:

IncludeReviseDeferReject

The committee at work

Completed VIS Restorative Principles

The committee's work produced a completed set of VIS Restorative Principles, published in March 2026. At their heart are eight shared beliefs:

1Relationships at the center
2We are all connected in community
3Everyone’s voice matters
4Emotions are important
5Restoration is collaborative
6Everyone has potential for growth
7Accountability builds community
8Reflection and action leads to change
They are accompanied by a shared-language glossary and age-appropriate versions for Early Years–Grade 2, Grades 3–5, and Secondary, with translations in Lao, Korean, Chinese, and Japanese so every part of the community can engage with them.

DEIJB · Professional Learning 2025–2026

Staff professional learning

All staff members included: a meaningful shift

This year, DEIJB professional learning was opened to all VIS staff, including operational and support teams. In previous years it was limited to teaching and administrative staff. The shift reflects our commitment to a shared culture of belonging across the whole community, recognising that every role at VIS shapes the experience of students and colleagues.

Session overviews and learning objectives
DEIJB: Identity & Power
Learning objectives
  • Develop a shared understanding of what DEIJB means in our VIS community.
  • Develop a shared understanding of identity and types of power.
  • Reflect on personal identity and power.
  • Commit to a personal action to use power for belonging.
Session slides and handouts
Warm Demander Framework
Learning objectives
  • Understand what it means to be a Warm Demander.
  • Understand and practice how to show strength, listen and affirm, and challenge and offer a choice.
  • Commit to a personal action to challenge when words, actions, and views cause harm.
Session slides and handouts
White Supremacy Culture
Learning objectives
  • Understand what "white supremacy culture" means.
  • Understand characteristics of white supremacy culture.
  • Reflect on how these characteristics live within us.
  • Commit to a personal action.
Session slides and handouts

What participants valued most

Facilitation quality

Calm, clear and welcoming delivery was praised across all sessions. Facilitators who shared personal stories and modelled vulnerability made participants feel safe to engage deeply.

Session design

Sessions were well organised with clear goals, strong pacing and an effective blend of visuals, independent reflection and small group discussion.

Language and inclusion

Lao language sessions were especially valued. Participants reported learning at a deeper level when content was delivered in their native language.

Personal and professional impact

Many participants left with new knowledge, practical skills and lingering questions, pointing to genuine engagement and meaningful learning transfer.

Reported barriers to full participation
Not enough time
Most common
Wanted more open discussion
Frequent
Role-play scenarios unclear
Occasional
Translation / language gaps
Occasional
Disengaged participant(s)
Rare
Suggestions for future sessions

Extend session time

The most consistent request across all three dates. Participants wanted more time for discussion and deeper processing.

Build a connected series

Participants want professional learning that builds on itself, pairing the Warm Demander framework with conflict and restorative justice concepts.

Differentiate by experience

Consider separate tracks for newer and longer-tenured staff, especially for the White Supremacy Culture session.

Clarify role-play scenarios

Warm Demander scenarios need more context and should model both the harmed and the harmer perspectives equally.

The Dreams in detail

Strategic Planning · Staff & community voice

Gathering community voices

One of our DEIJB goals (2.2) was to create an internal survey to gather data from all of our community members. The Quaglia survey VIS had used previously was not inclusive of everyone in our community. It did not gather feedback from our youngest students in Early Years to Grade 2, or from our operational staff.

In response, a new internal survey was created. This survey was translated into Lao for all community members. In addition, the Parent Voice Survey was offered in five languages, so every family could take part in shaping the strategic direction of our school.

Dream 3 · Inclusive Community · May 2026

What our community voices say

In our survey, parents, staff, and students were asked specific questions about how they experience respect, safety, accountability, and belonging at VIS. Here is what we heard, and where we go next.

526 voices in total

Three voices, one community

Parents 103 voices

Our most positive voice. Every question earned at least 83% agreement, with no area of serious concern.

Strongly positive

Staff 143 voices

A strong foundation of safety, inclusion and respect (84% of all staff responded), with a few specific areas to strengthen.

Strong, with gaps

Students 320 voices

Grades 1–12. Our youngest learners are very positive; older students are our most honest critics and see the most room to grow.

Most critical
Top 3 to celebrate
1

People feel safe and they belong

Physical safety and inclusion are near-universal among adults (97% of staff and 95% of parents feel physically safe) and strong for students.

2

Difference is respected

Across every group and every age, respect for identity, culture and language is one of our strongest results.

3

Our youngest learners are thriving

Grade 1–5 students see adults as fair and view mistakes as chances to learn, a sign our restorative approach is taking root early.

Top 3 to focus on next
1

Following through when harm happens

The most common concern community-wide: people don't always see harm addressed and put right (up to 1 in 3 secondary students). Make the outcome visible.

2

Feeling safe to speak up, across power

Around 1 in 3 staff and students don't feel safe raising concerns with people in authority. Build clear, safe pathways; have leaders model receiving feedback.

3

Repairing relationships after conflict

Every group flags this. We start the repair, but it isn't always seen through to rebuilt trust. Make the full cycle of acknowledgment, repair, and change visible.

Looking ahead · 2026–2027

Where to next?

We are a strong community with specific, fixable gaps, not problems to hide. Restorative approaches to harm and accountability will guide our DEIJB work together in 2026–2027.

DEIJB Community Focus for 2026–2027
4Using restorative approaches when harm occurs
Our community learning next year includes:
  • 4.1Building the practice of direct, accountable conversations using the Warm Demander framework and restorative circles.
  • 4.2Noticing and naming deficit mindsets and defensive behaviors.
  • 4.3Developing understanding of accountability as a community-building practice: understanding harm, intention, and impact, and the active steps of acknowledgment, repair, and change.
